Seminar Title:

Modulations in Dynamics and Thermodynamics of Martian Atmosphere Due to Dust Lifting Activities

Seminar Type:

Jagabandhu Panda

Abstract:

Martian atmosphere has attracted significant scientific interest since the beginning of space exploration. Dust is one of the most important components of the Martian atmosphere, intricately linked to its dynamical and thermodynamical evolution. The thesis work investigates several Martian dust lifting activities, associated dynamics, boundary layer processes, thermodynamical factors, and dust-related parameters to obtain a better understanding of the atmospheric responses to dust lifting activities by using observational and numerical perspectives. Two regional dust storms in Martian Year (MY) 36 were analysed to understand their growth and atmospheric modulations. Unstable atmospheric layers contributed to their formation while large-scale circulation supported their development. The storms also altered the near-surface meteorological conditions, including temperature, pressure, and relative humidity. The storms also modified the characteristics of dust devils and convective vortices by simultaneously enhancing turbulence while reducing temperature differences (between atmosphere and surface), resulting in complex changes to vortex intensity and their formation. Inter-annual variability of &lsquoC storms&rsquo during MY 33-36 displayed enhanced dust loading, atmospheric warming, and vertical transport, highlighting strong coupling between the lower and upper atmosphere. The MY 34 global dust storm (GDS) was found to suppress the formation of a subsequent regional storm by modifying the atmospheric thermal structure and reducing the availability of surface dust. The MY 34 GDS altered atmospheric circulation and solar insolation to the surface, altering the variability of atmospheric and surficial CO2 ice. While the surficial CO2 ice formation was hindered mainly across the southern hemisphere and tropics, the atmospheric ones were impacted mostly in the northern polar region due to the GDS. Overall, the thesis work provided new insights into the evolution of Martian dust storms and associated atmospheric variability across multiple spatial and temporal scales, thereby enhancing our understanding of the Martian weather and climate system.
